Slave Ship [5385]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
For more than 200 years the shipwreck of the São José Paquete d’Africa has gone undiscovered beneath the waves of one of the Mother City’s most popular beaches.

Jaco Boshoff, a marine archeologist, is one of the head investigators of the international Slave Wrecks Project, a global archaeological and research effort that began in 2008.

The project aimed to locate the São José based on archival documents of the Dutch East India Company that governed the Cape Colony until 1795, which were stored in the Western Cape Archives and Records Service.
After many failed searches near Camps Bay, the researchers reexamined the records and set their sights on Clifton Beaches.

An archival document found in the Arquivo Historico Ultramarino archive in Lisbon, Portugal, states that the São José left Lisbon on 27 April 1794 for Mozambique via Cape Town with 1 400 iron ballast bars in its cargo.
On 3 December 1794, Captain Manuel Joao Perreira sailed from Mozambique for Brazil’s Maranhão state. Perreira was planning a stop in Cape Town to take on provisions before crossing the Atlantic, where he intended to sell the 512 slaves. However, the ship ran into trouble off the Cape Peninsula and sank. More than 200 slaves died, while the survivors were sold into slavery in Cape Town.
in 2014 Persistence paid off and the wreck was discovered in the ocean close to Clifton’s 3rd beach and the first few artifacts were brought above water.


The top priority was to ready some of the artifacts – including the shackles, nails and cladding used for the ship’s construction – for a permanent exhibition on the São José that will open on 12 December 2018 in The Mother City’s Slave Lodge history museum.

On 2 June 2015, soil from Mozambique was deposited over the São José wreck site during a solemn memorial ceremony honouring those who lost their lives or were sold into slavery. The South African government has since declared the site a national monument.

It’s hard to believe that a rich time capsule of history lay below the locals and visitors of Clifton beach, waiting to be discovered for so many years

Slave Ship Script 3

Up sound under water

Jaco
“In Table Bay alone that there is about 500 historic ship wrecks we don’t know where they all are only about 5% of them have been located.”

V/O
There is still so much to be discovered.

Jaco Boshoff is a Maritime Archeologist, he could also be described as a treasure hunter, but he is more interested in the wealth of understanding the past, than finding gold or silver.

Fifty years ago, a ship wreck was discovered off the beach at Clifton.
In the 80’s it was speculated that it may be a Dutch East India Company Trading ship. Jaco and an international team, started diving the wreck again 7 years ago. They have found new artifacts, that shed a different light on it’s history.

Jaco
“diving on the wreck we realized that it couldn’t be the one they identified as it was too late. We found the ballast blocks, we found shackles.”

V/O
The shackles hinted at a darker history. Jaco spent many hours in the Western Cape Archives. After months his dedication was rewarded when he found a captain’s account of the wrecking of a ship called the Sao Jose Paquete d’Africa in 1794, during a treacherous Cape storm.

Link
The Sao Jose was a Portuguese slave ship that was headed from Mocambique to Brazil, transporting approximately 500 enslaved Africans.

V/O
We do not know what the ship looked like as there are only fragments left on the sea bed. What we do know is that the slaves were literally packed like sardines. Anticipating that some would die, the captors wanted to get the best return possible and filled the ship’s hold to the brim.

It is estimated that about 80 000 slaves were brought to the Cape over a 150 year period until slavery was abolished in 1808.

Link
“Soon after Jan van Riebeck arrived in the Cape in 1652, he realised that to supply passing ships with fresh food and sustenance and to build the infrastructure for the settlers, he needed a large workforce and that is how the slave trade began here.”

V/O
After 24 days squashed in the bowels of the ship, the Sao Jose slaves were dealt another blow when the ship ran into submerged rocks in Camp’s Bay.

Jaco
“On the night of the 27th of December the Sao Jose was hugging the Cape Coast because the captain was not certain of the conditions, as it was one of his first voyages around the Cape, they struck a rock because of variable winds and the ship eventually got stuck between two reefs. The crew saved themselves and in the process unshackled some of the slaves but they did not get to unshackle all of them and 212 slaves perished on the ship.”

V/O
Chained down with heavy shackles they had no way to save themselves.


Claire
“Why is the discovery of the Sao Jose wreck so Important?”

Tariq
“Well firstly and foremostly, it's a physical marker, on a very popular beach in a very wealthy area where there is actually a ship that has gone down and found it and brought things up. And that ship was carrying 500 slaves, 200 of them drowned there. So in many ways that is a sacred site for those of us believe that the wall is not solid between life and death. It is extremly important for one‘s ancestors. The 300 that survived were sold in Cape Town so they are our ancestors so what this event does is to stop and think.”

V/O
Tariq Mellet is a Historian and Heritage Activist. He has researched his genealogy and 26 of his forefathers and mothers were slaves.

Claire
“Can you tell the story of South Africa without including slavery?”

Tariq
“Absolutely not, the reason being every farm, town and city in this part of the world was built by slaves. The economy was built by slaves for almost 200 years and when you factor this out you literally factor out 3/4 of our history.”


Link
There are many places in Cape Town where one can still see the historical remnants of slavery, like the mosques in Bo Kaap and this the first slave church in South Africa on Long Street.

V/O
This plaque commemorates where the slave tree stood, the meeting point where thousands of slaves were sold.


Shanaaz
“My grandmother has passed on but she said to me “Ons was slave van Java” .Those were her words to me when I asked her where do we come from.”

V/O
Shanaaz Gallant is the curator at the Iziko Slave Lodge Museum in Cape Town where they have a permanent Sao Jose exhibition.The Lodge was built 340 years ago and possibly housed some of her ancestors who may have been VOC slaves.

Claire
“Tell me about the human rights violations they endured?”

Shanaaz
“The fact that they were chattel slavery, they were regarded as property. They were terribly violated and abused. There is extensive records for the type of abuse they endured, rape, severe beatings, torture, it’s a dark and ugly history.”


V/O
The majority of slaves came from African countries, but also from India, Sri Lanka and the Indonesian Archipelago. Literally creating our rainbow nation.


Jaco
“I ‘ve got an opinion that everyone whose family has been in South AFrica for more than 200 years have got slave ancestry. So I feel in a little way that I am telling the story of my ancestors to an extent.

Up Sound talk about the shackles

Claire
“What artifacts have you brought up?”

Jaco
“So far we have brought up some ballast blocks, we have brought up 1 piece of ship's structure, and a pulley block are on display at the Smithsonian Museum. We’ve got quite a few copper fasteners, and we have brought up some shackle, they are not on exhibition because they are so fragile. We are still busy treating those. We are planning to lift the cannon from the site.”

Claire
“Tell me more about the cannons?”

Jaco
“In the 1980’s a group of divers pulled up a cannon and left it on the side of the beach in Clifton. So we recovered that one, but they didn‘t preserve it so it is falling apart, we can’t tell much from that cannon and so we have one on a site that we want to lift and treat properly and conserve and that will probably tell us a little bit more hopefully about where the ship was built maybe.”

Up sound
“This is the ballast block to weigh down the ship.”

V/O
They were able to identify the wreck as the Sao Jose because the ship logs show they had hundreds of iron ballast blocks, to offset the weight of the human cargo. This is the first archeologically explored shipwreck in the world that sank with slaves on board.

Claire
“It’s been so long have you found any human remains?”

Jaco
“We haven’t found any yet. There is a good likelihood that it is possible but it's not something I can predict. The site quite rough.”

V/O
Although they have not found any bones yet, they have found bits of fabric

Claire
“It’s 2019 and why are we still finding it difficult to have a conversation about it?


Shanaaz
“There tends to be a silence around it and only once we start telling these stories do we break the silence and then people who descended from slaves start to understand who they are and where they are from and how strong our people were to have survived some of the ugliest things that man committed against another man. women and children.”

V/O
This is still an active dive, because the wreckage is strewn so far, it is going to take many years to uncover the secrets it holds.

Promo 1 x 10 secs
The Portuguese slave ship the Sao Jose sank 200 years ago off Clifton Beach. What archeological treasures have been unearthed and what does it tell us about our past?


Promo 2 x 15 secs
Over 200 slaves died here, on Clifton beach in 1794. The Portugese Slave ship, the Sao Jose was en route to Brazil and hit the rocks during a violent Cape Storm.
What LIGHT can the treasures that archaeologists are now unearthing SHED on those troubled times?


Promo 3 x 15 secs
Jaco
“In Table Bay alone that there is about 500 historic ship wrecks we don’t know where they all are only about 5% of them have been located.”
Maritime Archeologist Jaco Boshoff is part of a global team NOW unearthing artifacts from a slave ship that ran aground TWO CENTURIES AGO Clifton. How did 212 of the shackled slaves onboard die…and who survived?


Promo 4 x 30 secs NICE
Cape Town‘s Castle was built by slaves. Brought to the Cape at the behest of Jan van Riebeck, around 80 000 slaves formed his large labour force in the Cape. In 1794, a slave ship en route from Mocambique to Brazil ran aground in Camps Bay, carrying over 500 slaves, 212 died in the violent seas while still shackled in the hold of the ship. A global team of archeologists is unearthing artifacts that cast a new light on South Africa’s past.
